query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For multicomponent high‐entropy alloys at high temperatures, replacing traditional EAM references with a machine‐learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is actively trained on a diverse set of ab initio liquid configurations will improve the reference–target phase‐space overlap and reduce the thermodynamic‐integration path mismatch relative to TOR‐TILD’s EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: A multicomponent, equiatomic (or near‐equiatomic) refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., HfNbTaTiZr) in both solid and high‐temperature liquid states near its melting point (~1200 °C and above).
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an active‐learning driven machine‐learning potential (for example, a neural network potential) trained on ab initio snapshots that capture the full diversity of liquid atomic configurations.
generation.conditions: The methodology is applicable for HEAs with complex multicomponent chemistries (typically 4–7 elements in near‐equiatomic ratios) and high melting temperatures (≥1200 °C), where the liquid phase exhibits a very broad distribution of atomic configurations.
generation.structural_mediator: The MLIP acts as a configurational mediator by embedding short‐range order and disorder effects from the ab initio liquid, thereby bridging the gap between the simplified EAM reference and target ab initio phase space.
generation.mechanism: An active-learning MLIP trained on a wide and representative set of ab initio liquid configurations is expected to model the potential energy surface with finer accuracy. This increases overlap in atomic configuration space between the reference and target states, thereby reducing systematic errors in the thermodynamic integration path compared to an EAM potential that cannot capture the vast configurational diversity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The MLIP should reduce the thermodynamic integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, leading to more accurate free-energy estimates for these systems.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the current TOR-TILD approach which uses EAM reference potentials that inadequately represent the multitude of atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid, resulting in increased integration path mismatches.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only for multicomponent high-entropy alloys with complex configurational landscapes and high melting points (≥1200 °C). Simpler alloys or those with lower melting temperatures may not exhibit as significant benefits from this approach.
generation.uncertainty: While a 30–50% reduction in mismatch is predicted, the exact improvement will depend on the quality and diversity of the training data as well as the specific alloy system. Further benchmark studies are necessary to quantify the improvement precisely.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform thermodynamic integration calculations on a selected refractory HEA liquid (e.g., equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr) using two methods: one with the conventional TOR-TILD EAM reference and one with the new MLIP developed via active learning. Compare the free-energy integration paths over the same integration parameter and analyze statistical convergence.
measurements: Free-energy profiles along the integration path
Quantitative assessment of integration path mismatch (e.g., cumulative deviation metrics)
Statistical uncertainties in the free-energy differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP method does not achieve at least a 30% reduction in the thermodynamic integration path mismatch relative to the EAM-based TOR-TILD approach, or if the free-energy estimates from both methods do not differ significantly beyond expected uncertainties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the phonon heat conductivity and vibrational density of states in the refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr?. System: HfNbTaTiZr (equiatomic quinary refractory high-entropy alloy, bcc structure). Processing: Preparation of random bcc samples (128,000 atoms, 13.5 nm edge) followed by Metropolis Monte Carlo evolution with Kawasaki-type swaps (10 swaps per step, 100 K rejection temperature) for up to 4.7e6 steps to induce SRO; thermal conductivity calculated via non-equilibrium molecular dynamics at 300 K.. Test conditions: Temperature: 300 K (target); Monte Carlo temperature: 100 K; Simulation time for NEMD: 0.6 ns for gradient application, 0.4 ns for property calculation; Heat flux induced by thermostats at 0.8 T and 1.2 T..
